newsitem.title: LEBANON: Arab bond market seen at $500 bln by year 2000.
newsitem.headline: Arab bond market seen at $500 bln by year 2000.

text.p: The Arab bond market is expected to grow to $500 billion in total issues from the current $130 billion by the turn of the century, an expert on Arab bond markets told bankers on Thursday.

The drop in world yields was encouraging investors to look for higher-yielding instruments in the least-explored regions including the Arab world, Henri Azzam, an economist with Saudi Arabia's National Commercial Bank, said.
He told 400 financiers and bankers at an Arab Capital Markets Conference in Beirut that the Arab bond market was expected to grow at a much higher rate than stock markets.
"I think that by the turn of the century, we will have around $500 billion worth of bonds issued, most of which are expected to be issued by corporates," he said.
While most Arab stock markets were still closed to international investors, Arab bond markets were quite open to them, he added.
The current value of bonds issued by all Arab countries does not exceed $130 billion, Azzam said. Most were issued by governments.

The global value of bonds outstanding at the end of 1996 exceeded $3,000 billion, with 75 percent issued by developed countries, 11 percent by international institutions, 6.5 percent by offshore centres and 5-5.5 percent by developing countries.
"We are still scratching the surface," Azzam said.
"I don't think the future is bleak. On the contrary, I would imagine that over the coming few years we will seriously see a takeoff in the region's bond markets."
He said Qatar gas company which raised $1.2 billion on the international bond market in a few hours before producing anything, set an example for Arab corporations.
"This tells us that if certain corporates are borrowing for expanding viable projects, they should be able to get financing easily," he said.

"We have witnessed that international investors are more interested in our region than before, that international pension funds portfolio managements would like to diversify their risk globally," he said.
Among the immediate necessities was a government bond market that would provide a benchmark for corporates planning to issue.
"Corporate bonds would not exist without a government bond," he said.

The total outstanding government bonds in Bahrain did not exceed $1 billion. In Saudi Arabia it was $80 billion, most of which were in the books of autonomous government institutions and not the private sector, he said.
Foreigners could buy into bonds of Saudi either through banks or mutual funds, he said.
Some 45 percent of Oman's $1.1 billion worth of bonds have been taken by foreign investors while foreigners bought 15 percent of bonds issued in Lebanon.

Azzam said another priority was to create institutions which could price, underwrite, place and act like market makers for corporate bonds. "We need institutions that can provide custody, clearing and similar services," he added.
